title: Insertion Sort
directAnswer: For each element, shift the larger elements of the sorted prefix one step right and drop the element into the gap. O(n²) worst, O(n) on nearly-sorted input.

remember.takeaway: Insertion sort shines when the data is almost sorted.
remember.formula: for i: key=a[i]; shift a[j]>key right; a[j+1]=key

problemStatement: Given an integer array `nums`, sort it ascending using insertion sort (in place).
understanding: Grow a sorted prefix by inserting each next element into its correct spot, shifting larger elements right.

approaches.name: Shift-and-insert
approaches.whenToMention: This is the standard, expected solution — lead with it.
approaches.explanation:
Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix by taking each next element (the 'key') and **shifting** the larger sorted elements one step right to open a slot, then dropping the key in.

**Why it's great on nearly-sorted data.** If the key is already ≥ the prefix's last element, no shifting happens — so on an (almost) sorted array each insertion is O(1), giving near-linear O(n) total. This adaptivity is its real strength and why it's used as the base case inside fast sorts (e.g. Timsort).

**Why save the key first.** The shifting overwrites positions, so you must capture `key = nums[i]` before sliding elements, then place it in the opened gap at `j+1`.

**Stable, in place, O(n²) worst.** On reverse-sorted input every element shifts the whole prefix → O(n²); but it's stable and O(1) space.
hints: Treat the left part as sorted — where does the next element belong?
Shift larger sorted elements right to open a gap, then insert the key.
approaches.complexityReasoning: worst case shifts the whole prefix each time → O(n²); on nearly-sorted data few shifts → O(n).

java.explanation: Shift larger sorted elements right to open a slot.
Drop the key into its correct position.

pitfalls: Overwriting the key before shifting (save it first).

commonMistakes: Overwriting the key before shifting (save it first).
